title: Bulk text campaigns
like: the platform behind store coupons and delivery alerts, like Twilio or Braze
brief: Businesses send a coupon or an alert to hundreds of thousands of phones at once. Carriers accept texts only at a fixed speed, every text costs real money, and a person who replied STOP must never be texted again. Delivery receipts come back by the thousand and must be counted.

clarify.q: Can a campaign take a few minutes to finish?
clarify.a: Yes, within its window. Sending slower than the carrier allows is fine. Sending faster gets you blocked.

clarify.q: Can a phone get the same text twice?
clarify.a: No. Retries after a carrier timeout must not send it again, and a repeat is real money wasted.

clarify.q: What about people who texted STOP?
clarify.a: They must be checked before every send, and the check is audited. One wrong text can be a legal problem.

clarify.q: Do receipts have to be instant?
clarify.a: No. A few minutes is fine, but none may be lost or counted twice.

notes: Carrier throughput is fixed. Estimate peak sending rate before sizing the queue.
Each text costs about a cent, so a repeated send is a visible bill (approx.).
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

numbers.label: Texts leaving per second at peak
Cost of one repeated campaign of 500 thousand texts
numbers.how: 500,000 × about $0.01 ≈ $5,000 (approx.). This is why repeats must not happen.

hints: The carrier sets the speed, not you. What holds the work while it waits, and what makes a retry safe?
Queue the sends and let workers send at the carrier pace. An idempotency key makes a retry a no-op, and a consent check runs before each send.
Callbacks are evidence about one submission, not additional billable messages. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: The carrier is the narrow part, so everything before it is a line. Campaigns wait in a queue, workers send at the pace the carrier allows, and an idempotency key plus a consent check run before each text. Receipts take their own path through an event stream, so counting them never slows the sends.

designs.name: Queue at the carrier pace, key and consent on every send
designs.why: The queue absorbs the campaign and the workers drain it at the carrier speed. The key stops a retry from texting twice, the consent check honours STOP, and receipts flow through a stream into a time-series store.

tradeoffs: Sending at the carrier pace protects the account, but a huge campaign takes minutes instead of seconds.
Checking consent before every send is slower than checking once per campaign, and it is the only way STOP is honoured at once.
A second carrier raises uptime and speed, at the price of another contract and another limit to respect.
Counting receipts from a stream can lag by minutes, but it never slows a send.
editorial.realWorld: Carriers accept bulk texts at fixed speeds, often tens to a few hundred per second per connection, and each text costs around a cent. Big senders spread a campaign over time for this reason (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Bulk text campaigns: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Honor opt-outs at send time and reconcile billable carrier submissions. Consent can change while work waits; already-sent messages need an explicit boundary. Local deduplication cannot guarantee one external send without carrier support. Callbacks are evidence about one submission, not additional billable messages.

fields.label: Step 1. A recipient replies STOP after campaign enqueue but before send. What happens?
options: Trust consent captured when the campaign started
Recheck durable consent at dispatch and suppress the queued send
fields.explanation: Consent can change while work waits; already-sent messages need an explicit boundary.

fields.label: Step 2. The carrier accepted text M but its reply was lost. Retry how?
options: Reconcile M using carrier identity or supported idempotency, recording uncertainty otherwise
Send under a fresh id and count only one locally
fields.explanation: Local deduplication cannot guarantee one external send without carrier support.

fields.label: Step 3. A delivery receipt retries and arrives out of order. What counts?
options: Deduplicate receipt ids and apply permitted status transitions
fields.explanation: Callbacks are evidence about one submission, not additional billable messages.

correctness.responsibility: Honor opt-outs at send time and reconcile billable carrier submissions.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.
